title: Rappaccini's Daughter

teacherSummary.text: Student Giovanni Guasconti, lodging in Padua, watches Beatrice, daughter of the scientist Rappaccini, tend a garden of poisonous plants. He falls in love though her touch and breath kill insects and flowers. Professor Baglioni warns him and gives an antidote. Finding himself poisonous too, Giovanni turns on Beatrice; she drinks the antidote and dies, the poison having been her life. Baglioni cries out at Rappaccini's 'experiment.'

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Was this garden, then, the Eden of the present world” slowly and put it in my own words: Seeing the beautiful but strange garden, Giovanni wonders whether it is a modern paradise. Next, craft. I notice it is a question, not a statement, which shows his doubt. The strongest word is “Eden”: it calls up the biblical garden, and the temptation and fall that came with it. Then, effect. Why does Giovanni wonder if the garden is "the Eden of the present world"? My answer: The comparison warns us the garden is beautiful but dangerous; like Eden, it will bring a fall.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Sensitive content: Poisoning; death. Preview the story, tell students in advance, and allow a pass on reading aloud. Keep discussion on how the writer uses these elements, not on graphic detail. This section mentions drinking or a drug (“…specially when warmed by a flask or two of Tuscan wine. Giovanni, conceiving that men of scien…”). Treat it as period custom or plot detail; name it plainly and don't glamorize it.
